blocks.md: Should you spend a dollar today or save it for next year? Spending gives you the enjoyment of a little more consumption now. Saving gives you a dollar plus interest next year — but you value next year a bit less because of impatience. You are at the best plan when both options are worth exactly the same: the enjoyment lost by consuming one unit less today equals the enjoyment gained from the extra (one plus interest) units tomorrow. If saving were worth more, you should save more; if spending were worth more, you should borrow or save less.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the core condition of every modern consumption and saving model, and it shows exactly how patience, the interest rate and the desire for smooth consumption combine.
At an optimum the marginal rate of substitution between periods equals the gross return on saving:

blocks.tex: \frac{\partial U/\partial c_1}{\partial U/\partial c_2} = 1 + r \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad u'(c_1) = \beta(1+r)\,u'(c_2)

blocks.md: Maximize $U(c_1, c_2)$ subject to the [Intertemporal Budget Constraint](note:intertemporal-budget-constraint) $y_1 + \frac{y_2}{1+r} = c_1 + \frac{c_2}{1+r}$:
First-order conditions: $\partial U/\partial c_1 = \lambda$ and $\partial U/\partial c_2 = \lambda/(1+r)$. Dividing the first by the second eliminates $\lambda$ and gives MRS $= 1+r$.

blocks.md: **Reading it**: $\partial U/\partial c_1$ is the benefit of consuming one more unit today; $(1+r)\,\partial U/\partial c_2$ is the benefit of saving it instead. If MRS $> 1+r$, consume more today and save less; if MRS $< 1+r$, save more.
$U = \ln c_1 + \beta\ln c_2$ gives MRS $= c_2/(\beta c_1)$, so $c_2 = \beta(1+r)c_1$. Substituting into the budget:

blocks.title: Beyond the lecture
blocks.md: With $U = \ln c_1 + \beta\ln c_2$ and $f(k) = k^{\alpha}$, the optimal saving rate is constant: $k_2 = \frac{\alpha\beta}{1+\alpha\beta}\,f(k_1)$. With $\alpha = 1/3$, $\beta = 0.9$, $k_1 = 8$: saving rate 0.231, $k_2 = 0.46$, $c_1 = 1.54$, $c_2 = 0.77$, and MRS $= f'(k_2) = 0.558$. A chosen, constant saving rate — the assumption the [Solow Growth Model](note:solow-growth-model) simply imposes.

In an infinite-horizon planner's problem ([Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans Model](note:ramsey-cass-koopmans-model)), where capital depreciates at rate $\delta$, the same trade-off links every pair of adjacent periods:

The gross return on saving is the marginal product plus the undepreciated unit of capital; with full depreciation ($\delta = 1$) it is the two-period capital version above. In a steady state $c_t = c_{t+1}$, so the left side is $1/\beta$: capital must earn a gross return of exactly $1/\beta$.

- Writing $1+r$ on the wrong side: the MRS has period-1 marginal utility on top.
- Forgetting $\beta$ when computing marginal utility of future consumption.
- Treating the Euler equation as the whole solution: it gives the *shape* of the plan ($c_2$ relative to $c_1$); the budget constraint pins the *level*.
